overview.summary: Searching algorithms are used to retrieve information stored within some data structure.
learningObjectives: Understand Linear Search and its O(N) constraints.
Understand how data structures optimize searching.
Identify the best searching strategy based on whether data is sorted, mapped, or raw.
overview.interviewRelevance: Interviews rarely ask you to just 'search'. They ask you to design a system where searching is fast.

paragraphs: When you press Cmd+F to find a word on a page, the browser is running a string search algorithm.
Searching is so fundamental that computer science spent decades inventing Trees, Hash Maps, and Binary Search just to make it faster.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: The data structure you choose entirely determines the speed of your search. You cannot search a linked list in O(1) time, no matter how clever your code is.

definition.technicalDefinition: A search algorithm is any algorithm which solves the search problem, namely, to retrieve information stored within some data structure.

vocabulary.definition: Checking every single element one by one from start to finish.
The specific value or identifier you are looking for.
The total amount of data you have to look through.

keyProperties: Unsorted Arrays / Linked Lists: O(N) Search.
Sorted Arrays / BSTs: O(log N) Search.

metaphor: Looking for your lost keys. You have to check every room (Linear Search) because they aren't organized. If you always put them on the hook (Hash Map), finding them takes zero effort.
mentalModel.clickSentence: Optimization is just the act of organizing data so you don't have to look at all of it.

memoryDescription: Linear search requires zero extra memory. It just requires a loop.

operations.name: Linear Scan
operations.description: Iterate from index 0 to N-1 checking equality.
operations.visualNote: A highlight moves one box at a time from left to right.

patternTemplate.whenToUse: When data is completely unsorted and unstructured, or when the dataset is extremely small (N < 50) where O(N) is indistinguishable from O(1).

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: You need to find a specific user in an unsorted log file of 1 million entries.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: Because it is unsorted and a flat file, you have no choice but to use Linear Search O(N). Binary search requires sorting, and hash maps require pre-loading the data into memory.

examples.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
examples.problemStatement: Suppose an array of length n sorted in ascending order is rotated between 1 and n times. Find the minimum element.
steps: This is an evolution of search. Since it was originally sorted, we don't want to use Linear Search.
If mid > right, the minimum must be to the right of mid.
Else, the minimum is mid or to the left.
examples.rationale: This demonstrates how recognizing partial structure (rotated sorted) allows you to upgrade from O(N) Linear Search to O(log N) Binary Search.

conceptQuiz.question: If you need to search an array 10,000 times, should you use Linear Search?
options: No, you should either sort it first (O(N log N)) to use Binary Search, or put it in a Hash Map (O(N) build) for O(1) lookups.
Only if the array is small.
Yes, because Hash Maps use too much memory.
conceptQuiz.explanation: 10,000 queries of O(N) is O(10,000 * N). By doing a one-time upfront cost to organize the data, you reduce the queries to O(log N) or O(1).

practice.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
practice.keyInsight: Determine which half of the array is properly sorted, then check if target is in that half.

practice.title: Find Peak Element
practice.keyInsight: Follow the ascending slope using binary search.
